I'd love you to take me all the way back to where your first interest in investing in business

That concept resonated with me early on. It was rare that somebody picks up that material,
then they find a way to connect with Warren. Walk me through that story, how that all happened.
I started out writing to investors that I admired and respected, that I wanted to learn from,
CEOs of different firms on Wall Street. I wrote a letter to Warren asking to bring a group of
students out to Omaha. I had started a nonprofit focused on investment education for women.
He had had MBA students come, but he hadn't had undergrads. He generously said yes, and we
brought a group of students out to Omaha. What happened from there? I got to know him a little
bit through it, planned that trip three or four times. When I graduated business school, wrote him
another letter, asked if I could come out a day a week a month and pick his brain, assuming he'd
say no. Unfortunately, he said yes. I spent my post MBA summer working with him. In the summer,
he said, I'd love to hire you. I just don't have a role. Berkshire's 25 people at headquarters.
I started my full-time job, and he called a few weeks later and said, if you're interested,
I'll create a role for you to join. Quit my job and moved out to Omaha later that year.
What do you think it was, or maybe what did he tell you after the fact,
it's so rare that that would have happened, if at all?
Warren's always been very open at bringing people into his life at different stages. He was nearly
80 when I joined Berkshire. To trust me at that age was something special. I never asked him
specifically why. Probably a combination of grit, resiliency, willingness to work hard,
personality, those dynamics that came together. I had a number of people over the years write me
letters. Occasionally, they stood out to me too. My partner, Brian Humphrey, wrote me a letter when
he was in Stanford at business school. That's how I met him. For some reason, that letter resonated
with me in what he was sharing and was doing. It's hard to put your finger on it, but you know
it when you see it. If you're giving advice to people who are asking you about how to approach
someone that they admire, is there anything that you've been able to pull from the ones that resonated
for you? One is you want to try to find a mutual connection. You're from the same town. You're
interested in similar things, same school, same interests, being humble, being yourself,
definitely not using AI to generate it, not sending the same letter to 30 people,
customizing it, physical letters, were far more impactful than sending emails or connecting on
LinkedIn because that's so pervasive these days, it doesn't stand out.
When you showed up at Omaha, what was the job as the 26th employee?
I was Warren's chief of staff. I spent time working on anything that crosses desks looking at
investments. I worked on insurance deals, acquisitions, a variety of things. It was just an
opportunity for me to learn and grow, which was remarkable.
What did that feel like day to day?
There was a lot of responsibility. I joked. Warren had a few IQ points on me as well as
50 years of experience, so I had a lot to catch up on. I spent a lot of time reading,
learning, working late, trying to understand our businesses at Berkshire, why we invested,
and then what worked, what didn't work. Warren was very gracious to spending time with me,
going to lunch, talking about those companies in detail. That helped me become a better investor,
more thoughtful in what I was doing. The day to day work was what was coming across his desk.
It varied widely. It was going deep on a variety of topics that there was some need or some
interest on the Berkshire side.
How did your time there transition from pure investing to jumping into some of the portfolio
companies? When I was at Berkshire, I would travel and meet some of the companies. Warren
started asking me my thoughts on the businesses. The first was Larson Jewel, which is a custom
framing business. Then there was Benjamin Moore, Oriental Trading Company, Johns Manville,
and others. As I did that, Warren asked me to come in and a chairman role. Typically,
those businesses were once where the company wasn't operating to its full potential.
There was opportunity to help it. I'd come alongside management team, help them figure that
out and navigate it. In some cases, changing out the management team to help support that.
That was my first foray into operating. As I did that, what I realized was that there was
going to be more value created on the operating side going forward. In the buyout world, the days
of buying businesses for seven times and selling them for 12 a few years later was probably gone,
and you needed to add more value. I thought to myself, if I go get operating experience,
I'll be a much better investor. I'll have more credibility, more empathy, more ability to help
these businesses. That was the turning point in my mind of this power and this shift that was
happening in investing and operating. I'd love you to walk me through a story or two in your time
at Berkshire of those operating roles. Benjamin Moore, I was chair of that business. Benjamin
Moore is an amazing brand built over 100 plus years, tangible, sold through a dealer network.
Over a 10-year period, it had lost its way. Volume growth in terms of gallons had come down
considerably. Earnings were relatively flat. The business was cutting marketing spend,
taking price to maintain earnings instead of investing in the channel, investing in marketing,
investing in the brand, which is critical in that type of business. When I joined,
it was this opportunity. How do we reinvest in the core part of the business? If we do that well,
we can reposition the stores as leaders in their space. We can reinvest in our dealers
and see the specialness of that over the time we significantly improved the earnings of the business
while strengthening the channel, driving it through volume growth, not just financial engineering.
What did you see from going into the company to help them do that that was different from seeing
on paper that they had decreased marketing spend and there was less of a sell-through as a result?
Going into business is understanding what are the key drivers? What is influencing
management in their decisions and what they're doing? In that situation,
their incentives were misaligned. They were focused on how do I retain earnings versus
how do I reinvest in the future of the business? It became clear, we need to reinvest in the
future. What does that look like? In a business like that, brand is incredibly important,
getting awareness, visibility, that connection. They had cut brand spending and marketing spend.
The second is the store experience. When you walk into a store, what does it feel like from a
customer starting with that customer? What does that look like and how can we improve it? Lastly,
I would say it's always culture. There's oftentimes in these organizations where they've
declined. There's a cultural element that's got off track. In that case, it becomes stagnant.
They were afraid to make decisions. They weren't leaving the building. There was an
opportunity to reinvigorate the culture to help support those first two things.
In that example, what did you learn about what had happened over those 10 years that hadn't been
in place before that led to that period of time where you could change the inflection back up?
Going back and understanding and asking questions, why did we do this? Why didn't we do this? What
was happening along the way? I find when sometimes you take a step back and look at a 10-year period,
you can see stuff that each year you don't see. When you're looking at a business each year,
the little decline, a little decline, maybe it was the market, maybe it was some conditions,
maybe it was an anomaly. You don't take ownership of a decline. When you look over 10 years,
your volumes declined 10 plus percent. There's something serious going on here. Then you start
to dig in and say, why is that happening? Looking at those next level, and you can look at others
in the market. Sherman Williams had done a great job during this time period as an example.
What do we need to go figure out to improve that? In this case, the incentives were misaligned.
They had focused on the wrong part of the dealer in the relationship and the experience.
They felt like the dealer was waning. They started shifting away from the dealer instead
of leaning into the dealer. They were exploring other partnerships with big boxes at the time,
and that wasn't the right strategy for this brand, helping coming in, re-centering,
refocusing. Usually the answer is in the building. People know what needs to be done and how to do
it. Either you're not getting to it or you're not listening to it, or something else is influencing
the decisions that's leading to the wrong outcome. When you look at that example in the context of
everything you did at Berkshire, how did you think about managing your time? Warren always said,
if you want something done, give it to a busy person. It'll get done over time. I took on more
and more. I started on the investing side, became chair of each of these businesses,
kept those roles when I became CEO of Pampered Chef, wanted to go get operating experience.
When you're doing a lot, you start to realize what's most critical, how do you prioritize,
and how do you focus? That ends up being what's most interesting. Usually there's three to four
things that matter, and we get stuck doing all of these different things. The same thing goes
with an investment. There's three or four things that matter. We have a 100-page deck that goes
through all these other items, but if you know those three to four things, you spend your time
on those and you can get them right. Likelihood that you're successful is much greater,
with time is focusing on the things that matter most that are going to move the needle.
How about the distinction in your time from being chairman of several companies and then
CEO at Pampered Chef? When I was chair, what I realized was there is this opportunity to help
management teams and support them, but if you've never been in the shoes, you're always a step
behind. You needed to drive real earnings growth in businesses. If I could go be a CEO and get
that operating experience, I would have more experience that would help me in the future
with investing or working with management teams. I went to Warren and said, I like to be CEO
of Pampered Chef, which I was working with at the time. What I saw was there's a lot of opportunity
in that business. It had a strong brand. It had a strong channel. It had been under managed.
The transition from chairman to CEO was, for a lot of people, surprising. seldom do you see
investors go into operating roles. I felt like the future of investing was going to be operating.
I would be a much better investor if I went and got that experience directly,
gain that credibility, the empathy, the connection with these leaders that would resonate with
sellers in the future, resonate with management teams.
As you look at those different connections with the company from investor to chairman to CEO,
how did you think about going in for the first time, communicating what a plan would be?
The best way to go in is to go in open mind with more questions than answers.
Investors usually come in with answers. Here's our 90-day plan. This is what we're going to go do.
You don't actually get the best outcomes in doing that. We started Canberra with Listen and Learning.
How do you listen to people in the organization? How do you understand what's going on?
How do you ask the questions that are going to help you be smarter, but also further the
conversation? If you do that well, you'll get to a better outcome. You can co-create something
that's meaningful in terms of the strategy and the direction and the focus. That is far more
powerful than coming in with a plan or a direction.
What was different from what you expected of Pampercheff?
When I came in, I had been working with the business for about a year. I'd spent time
learning, listening. I had a strong view at that stage of what we needed to go do.
I told Warren, it would take me a year or maybe two years to get this thing coming.
It had been in decline for about a decade. It was a big turnaround that I needed to go do.
It ended up taking nearly four years to do it. Everything is harder and operating than it seems.
Even though I knew what needed to be done, I had the strategy in my mind. I knew I needed to go

Or you've got to work on culture and retention, which doesn't get changed overnight if you've had

Let's take margins from 10% to 14%. That's one click in my spreadsheet.
In reality, in a business, that takes a lot more work to do. There's a lot of missteps

Did you progress? You spend this time as a CEO. You could imagine being at Berkshire for a career,
going in and working with different companies, larger companies.
At what point in time did you decide you wanted to go do your own thing instead of doing it within
Berkshire? I was nearing the conclusion of the turnaround at Pampered Chef. We had the business
in a good place. I had met my now co-founder, Brian Humphrey. He had joined me as CFO there.
We were aligned from a vision and values perspective. I could be at Berkshire forever.
I'd have an amazing time there. It's a remarkable company. There's nothing like it,
and I don't think there ever will be. It was getting big in terms of capital.
It had $150 billion in cash at the time. Now it's $300 billion plus. It's hard to move the needle
with that size of check. What Berkshire had done 30 or 40 years ago was more interesting to me.
Buying businesses like Benjamin Moore, where you could partner with them, help them accelerate
the growth. What I'd seen in the market at the time was there was a growing group of families
and founders who wanted something different. They didn't want to sell the traditional private
equity. They wanted a Berkshire-like home, but they were just too small. There was this opportunity
in that moment to build something that was unique and different, that was solving a pain point.
Yes, I could stay here and be happy forever. There's also this opportunity to build something
special and unique that was differentiated in the moment.
When Brian and you decided you were going to do this, what did you lay out as the core tenets
of your philosophy having pulled from your experience as a Berkshire?
There were a few things that resonated with us that were important. One is long-term thinking
and a long-term structure. Oftentimes, long-term thinking conflicts with structure. Having those
two things together was important to us, and that was paramount to Berkshire, something we wanted
to replicate at Canberra. Second was providing that operating lens and that operating expertise.
We had built what is now the Canberra business system from the ground up, learning from greats
Dana Hearn, Marmin, and Toyota, Transtime, and others, taking those, applying them for
mid-sized companies. Lastly was this partnership mindset, working with families and founders
and coming alongside them. So much in traditional private equity is you get told what to do or
go drive this or hit this plan versus how do we co-create, build something special and unique.
That partnership mentality is core and critical to how we operate.
What did you do different structurally from the way private equity traditionally runs?
We did a longer-term structure. We have 15-plus years in our structure. The benefit of that is
it self-selects investors who are long-term oriented, which is beneficial. It's unique for
owners who say, look, I'm concerned with the three to four-year treadmill of private equity.
It gives them comfort that their business isn't going to be bought and sold and bought and sold.
It's that longer-term horizon that allows our management teams to focus on how do I build
this business for decades, not how do I build this business for a quick flip.
What do you find when you went into the market with that structure?
From an investor perspective, there's some investors it isn't a fit for. It doesn't match
their structure, their duration, their liquidity needs, which we understand.
There was a group of investors where immediately resonated with them.
It was aligned with how they think about building businesses.
A lot of our businesses will generate a fair amount of cash because they don't have a lot of
leverage. We can return capital. We have a business JM test. We've owned it three years.
We forexed the earnings in the business over that period and returned our initial capital to investors.
We still own our 70% plus of the business. That is a great model where, yes, there's
liquidity. It's not the same as an exit. We'd rather continue to own that business than back to it.
How did you encapsulate that idea of partnership?
There's a few things that we highlight. Structure is important, but it's one part
of the three-legged stool. There's a long-term structure that allows us to invest in these
high-quality businesses. There's our Canberra community, which is how we get to know companies.
We build relationships over the long term. There's the business system as we add value.
They all get mutually reinforced and powerful together. By having that longer-term structure,
our management teams can think longer-term. By our management teams thinking longer-term,
we can drive above-average returns. By having our Canberra business system, we can use it in our
community. By having that in our community, we get to know owners and CEOs well ahead of any
potential partnership. When those things start to compound on each other, you get the value of it.
It has been tough to communicate that story because it's not a simple, easy one.
Our belief and our competitive advantage is those things. That becomes stronger and stronger
over time and harder for someone else to come in and replicate. The most powerful part of the
story, though, is seeing it in the results. When we started a few years ago, it was a much harder
message to get it out there and able to communicate because it was a vision of what we were building.
It wasn't yet to come. You mentioned the Canberra community. What did you build to generate that
community? When I started as CEO of Pampere Chef, it was lonely. I had to go out and meet with owners,
meet with other executives to understand how do you manage a business effectively and well.
When I was doing that, I thought, wow, it would be so great to have a resource. Someone who could
come alongside me and say, this is what a great strategic planning process looks like or this
is how you can improve your executive hiring skills. When I started that journey, I realized
there was this need to help owners. They wanted to learn and grow and CEOs in particular.
So when we started Canberra, we brought that idea forward with this opportunity to get to know
owners and CEOs over time. We built the Canberra community to be that home that we wanted to
have in terms of learning and growing together. Now we have 4,000 CEOs in the community and owners
and C-suite executives where we're helping them with their business, taking a step back and saying,
this is what a great KPI process looks like. These are what the best benchmarks are.
That community relationship has been powerful and helpful for us. We learn about new spaces.
We get to know businesses. Most importantly, these companies get to know us.
We build trust and credibility. All of our investments have come through direct relationships.
Four of our seven have come through the community. We're building goodwill. We're building trust.
Even if the companies aren't ever going to take a partner or not interested in a partner,
what we find is they become great ambassadors for us. They share about Canberra with their friends,
other CEOs, and that's been powerful. How do you get from zero to 4,000?
We started with our first program. It's called Build with Canberra. CEOs apply to it. In our
first cohort, we had five CEOs we selected. Those first five CEOs recommended other CEOs.
We went out to our network and started inviting them. At the end of our first year in 2021,
we had 127 CEOs. It was still nascent at that stage. We went from 127 to 500 to 1,000 to 2 to 3.
When you add value, it becomes more of a referral community where people are inviting other people.
Now we've extended the programs. We have that three-month program. We also have a three-week
masterclass where you can go deep on hiring. We'll do three 90-minute sessions and help you
in hiring. We have webinars every month on different topics. We just did one on mission
critical roles. We started doing local and national events where we bring people together in
different communities in person so they can connect with other leaders in their regions
or in their areas. That has become more of a compounding nature where the relationships
become stronger. Our connections become more powerful. We get to build this trust with these
individuals. It's been a journey. It's been amazing to see the power of that, how many people engage
in it, how much they share, and bring other people into the community. What's the breadth
of what you've taught to these CEOs through the community? We start with our business system,
which is focused on how do you manage a mid-size company? It starts with people. How do you attract,
develop, and engage talent? Everything from mission critical roles in hiring to talent
engagement, communications, town halls to incentive plans, talent development, career
planning, career mapping, those types of conversations. Then we have the operating system,
which falls into how do you build a plan? What's your strategy? How do you resource that plan?
How do you think about capital allocation? How do you think about KPIs, budgeting,
all of those dynamics, and how you manage a business? Then we have operational excellence.
How do you continually get better and have better use of your assets, your costs, anything that you
have supporting the business, and then growth? Where's the growth in your business and what does
that look like? That's the core of where we spend our time. That helps probably 80% plus of companies.
They struggle with topics within that. Each business is different. For one, it might be hiring. For
another, it might be KPIs. We're helping them in that. There's other topics we've expanded out
by demand. How do I think about M&A? How do I think about developing a board? How do I think
about AI? How do I think about tariffs? We've led roundtable sessions as those topics come up.
We're sharing our own experience and perspectives, but we're also getting best practices and
learnings across the cohort and across the group. We learn a lot with people who are at the forefront
of what they're doing in their industry or on a specific topic. How have you nurtured and cultivated
the community once you've built it to that many people to make sure that people stay engaged?
Every month, we put a written brief out on topics that we're covering that we think are helpful.
The sessions that we're hosting virtually and in person that have those touch points.
Beyond that, it's those personal touches. We're thinking about you. You told us you were focused
on hiring and that was a tough challenge. Here's some new material as it relates to that.
Understanding where people are, touching base with them and connecting. Everyone is struggling
with something different in their business. As we get to know them, we can be more helpful in
doing that. Making connections might be you're looking for a board member in this space. We have
five community members in that space who might be potential board members or know someone.
Facilitating those introductions, connections, strengthens the power of the community.
There's a small firm. How do you scale your resources to be able to deliver that type of
customized experience across so many people? It's everyone's job to help support the community,
participate in events and what we're doing. It's core to how we operate and how we think.
That becomes second nature to everyone and what we're doing. Then we're thoughtful about how
to do it. We're going to be focused. Once we build the muscle, it becomes easier and it becomes
more scalable. Build with Canberra, the first program we launched five years ago. We constantly
improve it. The core stays the same. If we have a new cohort and new members, we're not changing
everything constantly. That allows us to scale and add on specific programs and initiatives that
are meeting our leaders and our CEOs where they are. I'd love to turn to how you leverage that
into your investing. You have all these people now in your network. What have you decided that
you're looking for of the companies that you may want to buy? We start off big picture on what
we're looking for, which is industrial services, manufacturing, some consumer. We're focused on
high-quality businesses. We're looking at businesses that are five to 50 million in earnings.
What's most important is the business model. Does it have a moat? Does it have a competitive
advantage? Can we see it quantitatively? Qualitatively can re-understand what's happening with that
moat. That's what we're focused on and what we're looking for. Anyone can join the community who
has a business over 10 million in revenue. A CEO of 10 million in revenue can join. By doing that,
we have a lot of people who aren't in our target space or what we're looking for and we're completely
happy to have them join the community. With the people that we get to know and that are interested
in their businesses or they're interested in a potential partner, we spend more and more time
with them. The days of auctions, it's transactional. It's not how most people think about their
businesses. If you've built your business over decades or it's a family business or your founder,
the idea of selling it through an auction doesn't resonate with a lot of people. You
care about your employees. You care about the future of your business. Price is important,
but it may not be the only thing that's important to you. It's the future value creation,
your legacy, how you're going to focus on customers. The relationships we're building
to the community we think are more powerful and over time, how more businesses will be
transacted will be through those relationships versus a traditional auction process.
We're going to take a quick break in the action to tell you about Brookfield.
Brookfield invests in the thing behind the thing behind the next big thing. Their focus
across infrastructure, energy, real estate, private equity and credit is helping to build
